analysis.title: ECB caught in the French drama
key_insights: ING expects the ECB to hold rates at its 29 October meeting and push any next rate hike decision to December, when new staff projections are available.

In September the ECB sounded more hawkish between the lines, with headline inflation higher for longer and core inflation expected to rise in 2027, which had set the stage for at least one more hike in December. Some had speculated about a back-to-back increase in October.
Headline inflation rose again in September and leading indicators point to continued eurozone resilience, so macro data alone would still justify another hike.

The rise in bond yields from the French fiscal and political crisis already acts as tighter policy. ING estimates the rise in German yields since the September meeting has had roughly the same growth and inflation impact as an additional 25bp hike, and for France closer to 50bp.

ING says three parameters will set the ECB path: the length and intensity of the Middle East war and oil prices, knock-on effects of higher energy prices on the rest of the economy, and a resolution of the French fiscal situation.
So far there has hardly been any pass-through of higher energy prices to the rest of the economy. If that holds, the need for more hikes drops. If it does not, the odds of hikes rise.
A French fiscal solution could bring relief to bond markets and allow the ECB to keep hiking. Without one, bond markets have taken over the ECB's role, making hikes less likely and less needed.

France will feature at the press conference even if it is absent from the policy statement. French spread widening has raised the question of ECB intervention through the Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI).

TPI activation requires the Governing Council to judge that the country pursues sound fiscal and macro policies, which in practice means compliance with the EU fiscal framework and at minimum full adoption of the proposed French budget. The ECB has kept discretion by saying criteria will be dynamically adjusted.

ING argues against early TPI intervention, since acting too fast for France could be seen by other member states as monetary financing of a country unwilling to follow the rules. Upcoming ECB leadership changes (Schnabel, Lane, Lagarde) could also affect the view on TPI.

ING expects a three-pronged response: a more dovish stance on policy rates, a temporary pause of quantitative tightening with flexible reinvestment of maturing bonds, and eventually TPI activation if contagion intensifies.
If France stays non-compliant with EU fiscal rules, ING says the ECB might consider buying bonds of almost all eurozone countries except France.
ING expects the 29 October meeting to be uneventful on action but not on words.

macro_indicators.interpretation: ING expects no hike, with any further hike delayed to December when new staff projections are available.
Higher headline inflation would on its own support another hike, but bond market tightening offsets it.
Part of the hawkish backdrop the ECB signalled in September.

macro_indicators.indicator: Tightening from higher German bond yields, hike-equivalent
macro_indicators.interpretation: ING's estimate of the growth and inflation effect of higher German yields, equal to one extra 25bp hike.

macro_indicators.indicator: Tightening from higher French bond yields, hike-equivalent
macro_indicators.interpretation: ING's estimate that French yield moves act like a 50bp hike, reducing the need for ECB hikes.

risk_factors: Prolonged Middle East war keeping oil prices high would raise the probability of more ECB hikes.
Pass-through of higher energy prices to the rest of the economy would raise the likelihood of new hikes.
Contagion in eurozone bond markets could force TPI activation.
A French fiscal resolution could ease bond yields and allow the ECB to resume hiking.
ECB leadership changes (Schnabel, Lane, Lagarde) could affect TPI policy.
vol_and_positioning: French government bond spreads have widened and bond yields have surged, in Germany as well as France, since the September ECB meeting.
geopolitical: War in the Middle East keeping oil prices elevated, with its length and intensity a key driver of ECB hike odds.
Fiscal and political crisis in France, with the proposed French budget not yet fully adopted and French spreads widening.

key_data_points.metric: hike-equivalent impact of the rise in French bond yields
key_data_points.anchor: For France, it's closer to a 50bp hike.

key_data_points.metric: date of next ECB meeting, no hike expected
key_data_points.context: Next rate hike decision seen delayed to December
key_data_points.anchor: The European Central Bank meeting on 29 October is not expected to result in an interest rate hike.

tension_points.bull_case: Higher headline inflation in September, resilient eurozone growth indicators and expected core inflation increase in 2027 would justify another hike, possibly in December.
tension_points.bear_case: The surge in bond yields from the French crisis already tightens policy by about 25bp for Germany and 50bp for France, so the bond market has taken over the ECB's job and hikes become less needed.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Pass-through of higher energy prices to the rest of the economy, or a prolonged Middle East war keeping oil elevated, would raise hike odds. A French fiscal solution that eases bond yields would also allow the ECB to continue hiking.

theme_stances.key_argument: The surge in bond yields from the French crisis already imposes a restrictive stance, so the ECB is very likely to stay on hold and delay any hike to December.
theme_stances.evidence: the bond market has taken over the ECB's job

theme_stances.key_argument: Intervening too quickly in support of France may be seen as monetary financing of a country unwilling to follow the rules, which argues against early TPI use.
theme_stances.evidence: That argues strongly against early intervention.
